extracted.intended_audience: DHS policymakers, immigration officers, immigration attorneys, stakeholders responding to the public charge NPRM
extracted.subtask_description: Regulatory standards and guidance for making public-charge inadmissibility determinations under INA section 212(a)(4), including what factors officers must consider, how to weigh them (totality of the circumstances), definitions used by prior rules, and related public charge bond rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory minimum factors (age, health, family status, assets/resources/financial status, education and skills)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 212(a)(4)(B) of the INA lists the minimum, non-exhaustive list of factors the consular officer or immigration officer must consider when making a public charge inadmissibility determination: the alien's age; health; family status; assets, resources, and financial status; and education and skills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statute states officers "shall at a minimum" consider these five factors, indicating Congress intended these to be baseline considerations and not an exhaustive list. Officers must assess these in the context of the totality of the circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavit of Support under section 213A
rubrics_metrics.description: In addition to the five statutory factors, the consular officer or immigration officer may also consider any Affidavit of Support under section 213A of the INA when making a public charge inadmissibility determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where an Affidavit of Support is required, it is a specific additional factor that officers should evaluate as part of the totality of the circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Totality of the circumstances / prospective individualized analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Public-charge inadmissibility determinations are made on a case-by-case basis in the context of the totality of the circumstances; the adjudicating officer must weigh both the positive and negative factors when determining likelihood that someone might become a public charge. The determination of financial responsibility should be a prospective evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Officers should weigh positive and negative evidence, assess future likelihood of dependence on public resources, and consider all relevant case-specific information rather than applying a mechanistic rule. Past USCIS/INS guidance repeatedly emphasizes fact-specific, discretionary determinations and that every denial should reflect consideration of these factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Officer discretion and authority to consider case‑specific additional factors (catch‑all)
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress' use of "shall at a minimum" signals officers may consider case-specific additional factors; DHS argues regulations should not limit officers to a finite list and should permit officers to consider other factors relevant to any individual case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The NPRM asserts the 2019 and 2022 Final Rules wrongly "straitjacket" officers by enumerating exclusive factors. DHS proposes removing regulatory text that precludes consideration of other relevant facts so officers can exercise statutorily-mandated discretion tailored to the specific facts of a given case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of receipt of public benefits (types of benefits to be considered)
rubrics_metrics.description: Past rules limited which public benefits could be considered (2019: a list including Federal/State/local/tribal cash assistance, SNAP, Section 8, most Medicaid, Public Housing; 2022: limited to public cash assistance for income maintenance and long-term institutionalization). DHS proposes eliminating those narrow lists and permitting consideration of receipt of any type of public benefits relevant to whether an alien lacks self-sufficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS states excluding benefits such as SNAP, CHIP, Medicaid (other than long‑term institutional services), and housing benefits is inconsistent with PRWORA and congressional intent. Officers should be able to consider dependence on other benefits that meet basic necessities or impose similar aggregate costs as cash assistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition (by 2022 rule) on considering benefits received by dependents (bright-line rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 2022 Final Rule stated a bright-line rule prohibiting consideration of the receipt of public benefits by an alien's dependents, such as a U.S. citizen child in a mixed-status household.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The NPRM notes this bright-line prohibition existed in the 2022 Final Rule (87 FR 55472, 55474) but characterizes the 2022 rule overall as unduly restrictive and proposes removal of the regulatory framework that included such limitations. Whether and how to treat dependents' receipt of benefits is thus a contested policy element discussed in the NPRM.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions of 'likely at any time to become a public charge' (2019 rule: >12 months in 36-month period)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 2019 Final Rule defined a public charge as "an alien who receives one or more public benefits... for more than 12 months in the aggregate within any 36-month period (such that, for instance, receipt of two benefits in one month counts as two months)." It defined "likely at any time to become a public charge" as "more likely than not at any time in the future to become a public charge" based on the totality of circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS finds the 2019 temporal/benefit-counting definition too restrictive and proposes to remove such bright-line temporal thresholds to allow more flexible, individualized assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'likely at any time to become a public charge' (2022 rule: primarily dependent on government)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 2022 Final Rule defined "likely at any time to become a public charge" to mean "likely at any time to become primarily dependent on the government for subsistence, as demonstrated by either the receipt of public cash assistance for income maintenance or long-term institutionalization at government expense."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS proposes to eliminate the 2022 definition as overly narrow, arguing that aliens may lack self-sufficiency without being primarily dependent on government, and that no statute or case law prescribes the precise degree or threshold of benefit receipt that makes someone a public charge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement that determination and denials reflect consideration of factors and articulate reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: Earlier guidance (e.g., 1999 Interim Field Guidance) emphasized: "Every denial order based on public charge must reflect consideration of each of these factors and specifically articulate the reasons for the officer's determination."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS cites this as consistent with statutory intent and past practice; removals or changes to regulations should preserve the expectation that adjudicators document consideration of relevant factors and explain their reasoning in denials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of disability, long‑term institutionalization, and other specific adverse circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Agency guidance and case precedent have directed that certain circumstances—such as mental or physical disability, advanced age, or long-term institutionalization at government expense—may be facts 'reasonably tending to show that the burden of supporting the alien is likely to be cast on the public' and thus can be adverse factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: USCIS/INS materials and fact sheets (e.g., 2009, 2011, historical INS articles) are cited to support considering clinical findings, medical certificates, testimony, and other evidence in medical cases and to treat long-term institutional care as potentially adverse in the totality analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public charge bond breach, cancellation, and appeal rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed amendments to 8 CFR 103.6(c): a public charge bond will be canceled when the alien dies, departs permanently, or is naturalized (provided the alien did not breach the bond). Under proposed 8 CFR 103.6(c)(1)(B), a bond submitted on or after the effective date would be breached if the bonded alien receives any means-tested public benefits prior to death/permanent departure/naturalization or otherwise violates a bond condition. Bonds accepted before the effective date remain subject to the standards in effect when accepted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS proposes to replace language that referenced receipt of public cash assistance or long-term institutionalization as breach triggers with broader language (receipt of any means-tested public benefits). The proposal also clarifies that final breach determinations are appealable by sureties and by aliens (8 CFR 103.6(f), 103.3). DHS will remove misleading language suggesting DHS may cancel a bond by determining post-adjudication that an alien 'is not likely at any time to become a public charge.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence types and investigatory practices in medical and other factual cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical INS guidance describes the proof in medical/public-charge cases: Form I-234 evidence, clinical findings, medical certificates, testimony of the alien, relatives, or friends, facts about cause of disability, status at last entry, length of residence before institutionalization, and social characteristics (age, marital status, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These examples support that public-charge determinations can and should rely on documentary and oral evidence specific to the case, and that officers historically conducted careful investigations before acting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alignment with congressional intent and PRWORA's self‑sufficiency goal
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS frames the guiding standard as Congress' policy in PRWORA that 'aliens within the Nation's borders not depend on public resources to meet their needs, but rather rely on their own capabilities and the resources of their families, their sponsors, and private organizations.' DHS contends regulations should be interpreted and applied to implement that objective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS argues narrow regulatory definitions and finite lists of benefits impede implementation of PRWORA and the INA, and that DHS should be able to consider evidence that an alien lacks self-sufficiency even if they are not 'primarily dependent' as phrased in the 2022 rule.
